claims.text: Presumed consent: applies when immediate decisions are medically required, the patient is incapacitated, and an authorized surrogate is not immediately available.
claims.quote: When immediate decisions are medically required, the patient is incapacitated, and an authorized surrogate is not immediately available, the doctrine of presumed consent applies.

claims.text: Minors: in most states, children below the age of 18 years cannot legally give medical consent, so most nonemergency care cannot proceed without a parent’s or guardian’s consent.
claims.quote: In most states, children below the age of 18 years do not have the legal capacity to give medical consent. Therefore, for most nonemergency medical decisions affecting minors, medical care cannot proceed without a parent’s or guardian’s consent.

claims.text: Exceptions for minors: emancipated minors can consent to all medical treatments, and in most states minors can consent to certain treatments (eg, sexually transmitted infections, birth control prescriptions, drug and substance use, mental health) without parental permission; individual state law must be consulted.
claims.quote: First, emancipated minors can consent to all medical treatments on their own behalf. Second, in most states, minors can consent to certain medical treatments (eg, treatment of sexually transmitted infections, prescriptions for birth control, treatment of drug and substance use, mental health treatment) without parental permission. Individual state law must be consulted.

claims.text: Adults who lack capacity: unless the patient has a clearly applicable advance directive or POLST, clinicians must rely on an authorized surrogate.
claims.quote: When adult patients lack capacity to consent to or refuse medical treatment, unless the patient has a clearly applicable advance directive or POLST, health care professionals must rely on an authorized surrogate for consent and decision making.

claims.text: Court-appointed guardian or conservator: if one has authority to make health care decisions, that person is the authorized surrogate.
claims.quote: If adult patients already have a court-appointed guardian or conservator (both court-appointed surrogates) with authority to make health care decisions, that court-appointed surrogate is the authorized surrogate.

claims.text: Health care agent: the agent or proxy named in a durable power of attorney for health care can make decisions within the scope that document grants.
claims.quote: If patients who lack capacity have a durable power of attorney for health care (typically part of an advance directive), the agent or proxy appointed by that document is authorized to make health care decisions within the scope of authority granted by the document.

claims.text: Default surrogate: with neither, clinicians usually rely on the next of kin or even a close friend; the typical priority is spouse or domestic partner, adult child, parent, sibling, then possibly other relatives or a close friend, and the priority varies by state.
claims.quote: If patients have neither a court-appointed surrogate (guardian or conservator) nor a self-appointed surrogate (agent or proxy), then health care professionals usually rely on the next of kin or even a close friend as the default surrogate decision maker. Most states authorize default surrogate decision makers; however, the exact scope of authority and the priority of permissible surrogates vary by state. Their typical order of priority is a spouse or domestic partner, an adult child, a parent, a sibling, and then possibly other relatives or a close friend.

claims.text: Surrogates’ duty: follow the patient’s expressed wishes and act in the patient’s best interests.
claims.quote: have an obligation to follow the expressed wishes of the patient and to act in the patient’s best interests
